title: When the stock market has a rough day, I check my plan instead
dek: Stocks fell Monday and the 10-year Treasury yield hit a 19-year high, which is a good moment to stay calm and look at your own plan.
keywords: what to do when stocks fall
body: If you looked at your retirement account after Monday, you may have felt a small drop in your stomach. The S&P 500 fell 0.77 percent, the Nasdaq fell 0.92 percent, and the Dow fell 0.67 percent as oil prices rose and tensions overseas grew.

The 10-year Treasury yield also reached 5.2 percent, its highest level in 19 years. That number can sound abstract, but it tends to show up in real life through the interest rates people pay on things like mortgages and loans.

I am not a financial advisor, and I cannot tell anyone what to do with their money. What I have learned for myself is that reacting to one day of headlines rarely helps me. When markets get shaky, I try to look at my own plan instead of the ticker.

That means asking simple questions. Do I have some savings set aside for emergencies? Is my timeline for this money years away or months away? Those answers matter more to my decisions than one rough Monday.
This afternoon, spend ten minutes looking at your own savings plan, and write down one question you want to ask a professional about it.
